steps.explanationAfterStep: Breaking the secondary C–H gives the more stable secondary radical. But the H–Cl bond formed (431 kJ mol⁻¹) is stronger than any C–H bond, so the step is exothermic and its transition state comes early, before much radical character builds up (Hammond). The difference in radical stability is felt only a little: per hydrogen, a secondary H reacts only about 4 times faster than a primary one.

Also correct: a primary hydrogen is taken. Chlorine is so reactive that this happens almost as often as the secondary route; there are three times as many primary hydrogens, so 1-chloropropane is about 45% of the product.
The secondary radical takes chlorine from Cl₂, and the new Cl• starts the next cycle.
The primary radical gives 1-chloropropane in the same way.

title: Chlorination of propane
subtitle: Cl• can take a hydrogen from the end or the middle carbon: which product wins?
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 37 (Radical reactions)

reactants.caption: propane + chlorine radical + Cl₂
hintTiers: Propane has two kinds of hydrogen: six on the end carbons, two on the middle carbon. Which C–H bond is weaker, and which radical is more stable?
The chlorine radical takes a hydrogen from the middle carbon, leaving a secondary radical. Three fish-hooks.
Chlorine's unpaired electron → new Cl–H bond; one electron of the middle C–H bond → Cl–H; the other → the middle carbon.
reactants.learnerPrompt: Use fish-hook arrows: each moves one electron. The chlorine radical takes a hydrogen from propane.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Bonding chlorine straight to carbon would give carbon five bonds. The radical abstracts a hydrogen, which can only make one bond.
Cl₂ does not react with propane directly. The chlorine radical is the chain carrier: it abstracts the hydrogen.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: One more fish-hook: the new Cl–H bond needs one electron from the C–H bond as well.
One more fish-hook: the new Cl–H bond needs one electron from the C–H bond as well.

propyl-radical.caption: propyl radical (primary) + HCl + Cl₂
hintTiers: The Cl–Cl bond is weak. What does the carbon radical attack?
The carbon radical bonds to one chlorine while the Cl–Cl bond splits evenly. Three fish-hooks.
Carbon's unpaired electron → new C–Cl bond; one Cl–Cl electron → C–Cl; the other → the far chlorine.
propyl-radical.learnerPrompt: The radical takes a chlorine atom from Cl₂.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: That reverses the first step. Cl₂ is in large excess and its bond is weak, so the chain goes on with Cl₂.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: One more fish-hook: the new C–Cl bond needs one electron from the Cl–Cl bond as well.

isopropyl-radical.caption: isopropyl radical (secondary) + HCl + Cl₂
hintTiers: The Cl–Cl bond is weak. What does the carbon radical attack?
The carbon radical bonds to one chlorine while the Cl–Cl bond splits evenly. Three fish-hooks.
Carbon's unpaired electron → new C–Cl bond; one Cl–Cl electron → C–Cl; the other → the far chlorine.
isopropyl-radical.learnerPrompt: The radical takes a chlorine atom from Cl₂.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: That reverses the first step. Cl₂ is in large excess and its bond is weak, so the chain goes on with Cl₂.

secondary-product.caption: 2-chloropropane (main product) + HCl + Cl• (carries the chain on)

mechanismSummary: Cl• abstracts a hydrogen from propane and the carbon radical takes Cl from Cl₂. A secondary C–H is weaker and gives the more stable radical, but the exothermic abstraction has an early transition state, so chlorine is unselective: there are six primary and only two secondary hydrogens, and the result is about 55% 2-chloropropane and 45% 1-chloropropane.
